tldr: By encoding a humanoid's structure, morphology, and dynamics as explicit descriptors and feeding them into a policy, a single reinforcement learning model achieves whole-body motion tracking across 4,096 different robot bodies from 16 humanoid families.
hero_caption: Overview of MimicAll. Starting from 16 humanoid templates, randomization generates 4,096 body variants. A single shared policy tracks diverse whole-body motions including aiming, crouching locomotion, running, and turning.
overview:
Whole-body motion tracking, which enables humanoid robots to imitate diverse human movements, has seen major progress recently. However, existing trackers are typically trained for a specific robot body. Applying the same motions to different robots traditionally requires retraining separate models from scratch, because joint structures, link lengths, mass distributions, and actuator response characteristics change completely.

The authors asked: "What if we provide explicit embodiment information—skeletal structure, geometry, and dynamics—as descriptors to the policy? Could a single policy control every humanoid?" To realize this, they proposed MimicAll. Structured embodiment descriptors automatically extracted from robot model data are transformed into global and joint-aligned conditioning features. These are injected into the policy alongside motion references and observation history. Combined with physics-consistent embodiment randomization, body-calibrated retargeting, and a memory-efficient windowed reference streaming mechanism, MimicAll enables joint reinforcement learning across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families at scale.

Evaluations on a standardized benchmark of 464 bodies show that this shared training significantly improves robustness against unseen morphological variations compared to single-body specialists. For instance, on randomized Unitree G1 bodies, a single-body specialist achieved only a 42.9% 30-second tracking success rate, while the proposed shared policy reached 99.4%. This research clearly demonstrates that proper injection of embodiment information is key to cross-embodiment whole-body control.
contributions: Designed structured embodiment descriptors that unify robot structure, morphology, and dynamics, along with conditioning mechanisms connecting them to control policies.

Built a scalable training infrastructure integrating physics-consistent embodiment randomization, body-calibrated retargeting, and reference streaming, enabling joint reinforcement learning across 4,096 robot bodies.

Established a standardized benchmark spanning 464 bodies and five strata, systematically analyzing embodiment descriptor benefits, four conditioning mechanisms (Concat, modulation, Cross-attention, Self-attention), within-family generalization, and unseen-family transfer limits.

sections.heading: New robot, new controller: How can we bridge embodiment differences?
sections.summary: To share whole-body tracking across different humanoids, policies must accommodate structural and dynamical discrepancies between bodies. This work presents MimicAll, using explicit embodiment descriptors to learn a single shared reinforcement learning policy across heterogeneous humanoids.
sections.details:
Humanoid techniques for reproducing dynamic human movements are advancing rapidly, but most existing methods train policies specialized for a single robot. When the robot body changes, joint topology, link geometry, and actuator torque limits shift completely. Following the same reference motion requires entirely different control commands.

Cross-embodiment learning, which shares control knowledge across multiple robots, has gained significant attention. Here, the authors focused on a fundamental question: what embodiment information should be exposed to the policy, and how should it interact with per-joint control? To address this, they proposed MimicAll, a framework that defines structured embodiment descriptors spanning Structure, Morphology, and Dynamics, converts them via encoders into global and joint-aligned conditions, and feeds them to the policy.

To train across thousands of bodies, they developed an infrastructure combining physics-consistent randomization, body-calibrated retargeting aligned with each robot's kinematics, and GPU memory-saving windowed reference streaming. This enabled large-scale joint reinforcement learning across 4,096 body variants derived from 16 humanoid families.

sections.heading: Where whole-body tracking meets multi-robot control
sections.summary: A review of deep reinforcement learning for humanoid motion tracking and multi-robot control across varied morphologies. MimicAll stands out by combining explicit embodiment conditioning with fully shared joint training.
sections.details:
To clarify MimicAll's position, four related areas are summarized:

### Whole-body humanoid motion tracking
Prior works such as DeepMimic, PHC, and HoloMotion successfully trained tracking feedback policies with reinforcement learning. However, they assume a single morphology. MimicAll builds on the MimicLite training stack while tackling the new challenge where both motions and the executing robot bodies vary.

### Cross-embodiment control
XHugWBC and EAGLE demonstrated shared locomotion and posture control across multiple robots. In whole-body tracking, works like VENOM, Any2Any, and X-WBC have emerged. In contrast, MimicAll avoids robot-specific sub-networks, fully shares parameters, and directly injects explicit numerical descriptors (mass, inertia, link lengths, etc.) into the policy.

### Embodiment representations and conditioning
Approaches like Hardware Conditioned Policies, MetaMorph, ModuMorph, and Body Transformer represent robot morphology via tokens or masked attention. MimicAll expands on these ideas by systematically dissecting which physical quantities to include, which encoder architectures work best, and where to inject them into the policy.

### Retargeting and reference consistency
Reference motions cannot be tracked if they violate the robot's physical kinematics. Drawing on works like GMR and OmniRetarget, MimicAll employs body-calibrated retargeting precisely tuned to each generated variant's forward kinematics.

sections.heading: Describing the body and wiring it into control: The architecture
sections.summary: Robots are mapped to 38 semantic joint slots, and physical properties are bundled into structured descriptors. These are encoded via Graph or MLP networks and wired into the policy through four conditioning mechanisms.
sections.details:
### III-A Shared tracking interface
To unify differing joint counts and layouts, MimicAll defines up to $J=38$ semantic joint slots. Existence masks $m_j$ track whether a joint exists, while action masks $m^{\mathrm{act}}_j$ track whether it is actuated. The policy outputs joint target angle offsets $a_t \in \mathbb{R}^J$, converted to torques via PD controllers. Observations include root angular velocity, gravity vector, and joint state history (0.32 s at 50 Hz), with reference motions providing a 0.08 s future preview.

### III-B Structured embodiment descriptors
The descriptor $e = (G, k, d)$ consists of three components:
- **Structure ($G$)**: Joint parent-child topology, joint types, depths, and semantic roles.
- **Morphology ($k$)**: Overall geometry (root height, collision bounding box) and joint-level nominal angles $q_j^0$, limit ranges, rotation axes, and relative transforms from parent links.
- **Dynamics ($d$)**: Total mass, center of mass position, inertia tensor about COM, link-level mass/inertia, PD gains, torque/velocity limits, and friction.

### III-C From descriptors to embodiment conditions
Encoders turn descriptors into a global condition $h_g \in \mathbb{R}^{64}$ describing the whole robot and joint-aligned conditions $h_j \in \mathbb{R}^{16}$ for each slot. Along with a Graph encoder performing message passing over the kinematic tree, a simple Flat-MLP encoder flattening all inputs into fully connected layers was implemented for ablation.

### III-D Incorporating embodiment into control
Four conditioning mechanisms were evaluated:
- **Concat**: A lightweight baseline concatenating $h_g$ directly into the input observation layer.
- **Adaptive modulation**: Adaptively modulates intermediate layers via scale and shift parameters derived from global and joint features.
- **Cross-attention**: Action queries attend to body tokens.
- **Self-attention**: Action tokens and body tokens are concatenated and jointly processed with self-attention.
The latter three mechanisms apply residual action corrections onto a base policy.

### III-E Joint policy and representation learning
PPO policy training is coupled with auxiliary tasks—descriptor reconstruction loss, cross-view consistency loss, and feature variance/covariance regularization—ensuring the learned representations directly benefit control.

captions.F4: The four evaluated embodiment conditioning mechanisms: (A) Concat, directly concatenating at the input; (B) Adaptive modulation of intermediate features; (C) Cross-attention where action queries attend to body tokens; (D) Self-attention jointly processing action and body tokens.

sections.heading: Engineering stable training across thousands of bodies
sections.summary: To jointly train across 4,096 robots and over 260,000 trajectories, the authors introduced physics-consistent generation, GPU-memory-saving motion streaming, and embodiment feature caching.
sections.details:
### IV-A Consistent generation pipeline for models and references
Starting from 16 base humanoid templates, link lengths and masses are randomized with coupled physical consistency to yield 4,096 body variants. For each variant, inverse kinematics (IK) retargets human poses to its exact geometry, and forward kinematics (FK) computes reference poses and velocities. Across 64 LAFAN1 motions, roughly 260,000 body-specific trajectories (2.93 billion frames in total) form a synchronized data bank aligning model descriptors, physics simulations, and reference trajectories.

### IV-B Shared runtime for heterogeneous simulation
Robots with completely different link counts and joint configurations are simulated in parallel within a unified training process. The shared semantic joint interface converts raw data to policy tensors and vice versa, seamlessly interleaving rollouts from diverse robots within a single PPO update.

### IV-C Windowed reference streaming and encoding reuse
Loading all 260,000 trajectories into GPU memory would cause out-of-memory errors. The authors implemented windowed reference streaming, fetching only the active trajectory time window from host memory on demand. Furthermore, because a variant's descriptor remains constant during an episode, embodiment conditions are computed once, cached, and reused during rollouts, drastically reducing redundant computation.

captions.F3: System architecture for cross-embodiment learning. Descriptors, motion references, and physical properties are consistently extracted from randomized robot models, enabling smooth data flow between parallel environments and the shared policy.

sections.heading: Benchmarking unseen bodies across five distribution strata
sections.summary: A 464-body benchmark was designed covering seen/unseen body variants and unseen robot families, establishing strict evaluation protocols for 30-second tracking success and tracking errors.
sections.details:
### V-A Five strata separating motion and embodiment generalization
To rigorously evaluate policy generalization, 464 robot bodies were categorized into five strata:
- **SS (Seen-Support)**: Training body variants sampled during learning.
- **SI (Seen-In-support)**: New body variants of seen families within the training randomization range.
- **SO (Seen-Out-of-support)**: Extreme variants of seen families exceeding the training randomization bounds.
- **UI (Unseen-In-support)**: Unseen robot families within their nominal generator range.
- **UO (Unseen-Out-of-support)**: Unseen robot families beyond nominal ranges.
Evaluations utilize 11 held-out LAFAN1 motion clips and 8 clips from 100STYLE, a completely separate dataset.

### V-B Control settings and metrics
Evaluations span 10 s, 20 s, and 30 s windows. A failure is flagged if position error exceeds 0.8 m or orientation error exceeds 1.6 rad in the robot local frame for 5 consecutive steps; the fraction completing the run is the Success Rate (SR). Additional metrics include Effective Tracking Time (Eff. Time), Global MPJPE (G-MPJPE), Local MPJPE (L-MPJPE), and Root Position Error (RPE). Whether the robot avoided falling (No-fall survival) is also tracked.

### V-C Controlled experimental conditions
For fair comparison, 10 configurations were evaluated using a fixed budget of 8 GPUs, $8 \times 8,192$ environments, and 10,500 PPO updates. They were also compared against a single-body specialist trained solely on the standard Unitree G1.

sections.heading: Results: Crushing specialists, but unseen skeletons pose challenges
sections.summary: Shared training vastly outperformed single-body specialists in robustness. Conditioning revealed a trade-off: simple Concat and Adaptive modulation achieved higher completion rates, while Self-attention minimized global tracking errors.
sections.details:
### VI-A RQ1: Robustness to body variations via shared training
On unseen style motions (100STYLE), the Graph + Concat policy achieved strong 30-second SRs across SS, SI, and SO strata: 97.1%, 92.3%, and 91.9%, respectively. The high success rate in the out-of-distribution SO stratum validates the power of embodiment descriptors.
The comparison against single-body specialists was striking. A specialist trained only on nominal G1 saw its 30-second SR plummet to 42.9% across 24 randomized G1 bodies. In contrast, the MimicAll shared policy trained on all robots with the same total environment transitions achieved an impressive **99.4%** success rate. Training across diverse bodies simultaneously induces deep robustness to morphological shifts.

### VI-B RQ2: Which embodiment details and conditioning mechanisms matter?
- **Descriptor content**: Using only "Structure + Morphology" (89.7%) or only "Dynamics" (89.0%) lagged behind the full descriptor (91.9% on 100STYLE SO). Integrating all components becomes crucial under large bodily shifts.
- **Encoder scale**: Matching parameter counts, the complex Graph encoder and the compact Flat-MLP (42) achieved similar SRs (91.9% vs. 91.4% on 100STYLE SO). Highly structured graph models are not strictly necessary; a compact MLP leverages embodiment information effectively.
- **Conditioning trade-offs**: While Concat and Adaptive modulation favored raw tracking completion (SR), **Self-attention** achieved the lowest global position errors (G-MPJPE of 660.7 mm on LAFAN1 vs. 958.2 mm for Mask-only) and root position errors (RPE).
- **Causal validation via intervention**: In the Self-attention model, providing true body conditions yielded 61.7% SR, swapping to mismatched conditions dropped SR to 47.0%, and zeroing conditions dropped it to 33.7%. This 14.7-point drop confirms that the policy relies on embodiment information in closed-loop feedback.

### VI-C RQ3: Transfer limits and target specialization
While dominant within seen families, policies transferred poorly to entirely unseen families (UI/UO), with LAFAN1 SR dropping below 8.2%. Descriptor reconstruction accuracy remained high at the joint level ($R^2 \approx 0.73\text{--}0.79$) but plunged at the global body level ($R^2 \approx 0.34\text{--}0.38$), highlighting the difficulty of coupling novel skeletal topologies with known joint dynamics.
However, taking a shared checkpoint trained for 5,000 updates and fine-tuning solely on nominal G1 for 5,500 updates halved G-MPJPE from 1201.4 mm to 545.4 mm, outperforming the scratch specialist.

captions.F12: The same Self-attention policy tracking identical motions on G1 variants with widely differing masses: 20.6 kg (SS), 21.3 kg (SI), and 40.1 kg (SO). Semi-transparent blue shows the reference pose; tracking remains stable even when body mass is doubled.

sections.heading: Paving the path toward generalist humanoid foundation policies
sections.summary: MimicAll proves that large-scale shared training with explicit embodiment descriptors brings unprecedented robustness to humanoid morphological variations. Remaining transfer challenges to unseen families point to key future directions.
sections.details:
In summary, MimicAll demonstrates that thousands of humanoid variants can be controlled using a single reinforcement learning policy. A vital architectural insight is the trade-off between control objectives: simple concatenation suffices for motion completion, whereas dense interaction mechanisms like Self-attention are critical for suppressing drift and accurately tracking global positions.

Furthermore, the finding that training on a single robot fails to handle body variations, while joint learning across diverse robots produces genuine robustness, provides a key takeaway for future humanoid foundation models.

The main remaining challenge is zero-shot transfer to unseen skeletal families. While adapting to within-family variations succeeds, generalizing to unseen joint topologies will require expanding the diversity of training humanoid families. Future work will extend this framework to contact-rich motions and real-world robot deployment.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details and extra visualizations
sections.summary: Details on the 38-slot joint mapping, auxiliary loss weightings, continued training protocols, and qualitative tracking visualizations across all 16 humanoid families.
sections.details:
### Implementation and network details
The shared interface uses continuous descriptor fields of 18 dimensions for the full robot and 31 dimensions per joint, totaling 1,196 dimensions excluding categorical masks. The Graph encoder uses 3 attention blocks with width 128 and 4 heads, outputting a 64-dimensional global condition and 16-dimensional joint conditions. The backbone MLP uses 3 layers of width 256, the residual MLP uses 3 layers of width 1024, and PPO optimization is wrapped with Muon/AdamW.

### Continued training and difficulty-based sampling
For Flat-MLP (256), continuing training from 10,500 to 12,500 updates on the Train49 dataset (excluding obstacle motions) boosted LAFAN1 SR from 67.6% to 71.7%. Motion phase-based difficulty sampling was also shown to further enhance tracking accuracy.

### Multi-robot tracking visualizations
Appendix figures F10 and F11 demonstrate that all 16 robot families—including Booster K1/T1, Agibot X2, Fourier N1, LimX D03/D04, and Unitree G1—perform walking, running, kicking, and crouching locomotion using a single shared checkpoint (Flat-MLP (256) + Concat).

captions.F10: Simulation results of the first 8 humanoid families executing diverse motions (turning, walking, crouching locomotion, kicking, backward walking, running) controlled by a single shared checkpoint (Flat-MLP 256 + Concat).

takeaways: Supplying explicit descriptors of mass, inertia, and geometry to a policy enables a single shared model to control diverse humanoid robots across whole-body motions.
Given the same compute budget, joint training across diverse body variants yields vastly superior robustness to body shifts compared to single-robot specialists (99.4% vs. 42.9% success).
Concat and Adaptive modulation excel at motion completion rates, while Self-attention achieves the lowest global position errors.
Pre-training a shared policy across multiple bodies followed by fine-tuning on a specific robot achieves higher tracking precision than training a specialist from scratch.
limitations: Zero-shot transfer success to completely unseen robot families with novel joint topologies remains low (below 10%), currently limiting generalization to within-family variations.
Evaluations were conducted solely in simulation; addressing the sim-to-real gap and validating whole-body tracking on physical humanoids remains future work.
Complex contact transitions, including obstacle traversal, uneven terrain, and deliberate environment contacts (e.g., placing hands on surfaces), were excluded from the scope.
